## AEP 1: Hammerfest System

Exposure data were filtered to the Hammerfest coastal area. 13 groups were returned, with data dominated by national monitoring campaigns (see [@tbl-groups-a001], SI). Based on @comberSourcesCopperEuropean2023 and available data for the region, six source KES were included: natural run-off, anthropogenic run-off, and vessel antifoulants (without quantified emissions) and industrial emissions, WWTP discharge, and aquaculture emissions (quantified). 

Mapping measured copper concentrations in the Hammerfest area (@fig-aep1-conc) revealed a spatially specific pattern of both monitoring and exceedance of background/threshold levels. Most measurements were conducted at aquaculture facilities or in the Hammerfest harbour area. Marine sediment concentrations were largely at Background/Good levels across the area, although points in the vicinity of aquaculture facilities at Eidvåget and Kommagnes in the south-west of the area showed occasional Poor or Very Poor concentrations (based on Norwegian EQS values [@norwegianenvironmentagencyThresholdsClassificationWater2020]). Copper concentrations in *G. morhua* livers and *M. edulis* above PROREF were detected around Hammerfest harbour, and on the NW coast of Melkøya, home to Hammerfest LNG plant. No pattern of contamination in sites closer to the Repparfjord (south-east corner) was observed. Occasional freshwater sampling sites were also present (e.g. the site marked "lufthavn" to the east of Hammerfest, which despite the name is not an airport). These points were excluded from consideration.

![Copper concentration data in the Hammerfest coastal system (AEP 1). Points shaped by sample group and coloured by worst measured concentration relative to (M-608) EQS or PROREF as appropriate. Red rectangle: AEP bounding box, Black stars: PRTR facilities, Blue circles: licensed aquaculture locations.](figures/fig06-aep1-concentrations.png){#fig-aep1-conc}

A simple assessment (@fig-a001-timeseries) of copper concentrations in key sampling groups (*G. morhua* liver, blue mussels, coastal water and marine sediment) showed no obvious time trend. Cod liver concentrations only occasionally exceed PROREFs (in 2014, 2015 and 2024). Blue mussel whole body concentrations are orders of magnitude higher in 2011 (also present in the source data); however, measurements in 2019 and 2024 continue to show many PROREF exceedances. Measurements in coastal water are insufficient to detect a trend. Sediment concentrations appear roughly steady over the measured time period, although a lack of Very Poor (EQS) copper concentrations after 2022 is notable (likely due to the harbour clean-up project). 

![Measured copper concentrations in specific compartments/organisms/tissue (with group numbers) over time in the Hammerfest coastal system (AEP 1). Points coloured by EQS class/PROREF exceedance as appropriate. Dashed horizontal lines mark EQS/PROREF thresholds. Dotted vertical line (2024) marks end of Hammerfest harbour cleanup project. dw: dry weight, ww: wet weight.](figures/fig09-aep1-timeseries.png){#fig-a001-timeseries}

[@fig-hammerfest-aep] shows a proposed AEP for the Hammerfest coastal system. Copper flows to the environment from a variety of anthropogenic and natural sources, of which only WWTP discharge, aquaculture and emissions from industrial facilities are to some degree quantified. Flows of copper to receiving water and sediment are generally highly plausible but poorly evidenced, and insufficient information is available to assess their essentiality (i.e. if interrupting any specific source would change measured concentrations). 

Modelled copper emissions (kg/year) per aquaculture facility are reported for 8 of the facilities in Hammerfest municipality, albeit without metadata or methodology available. Reported copper emissions were summed across registered facilities within the study area ([@fig-aquaculture-emissions]) and a mean calculated across the period (89.9 kg/year). Because it is uncertain how accurately these figures represent actual emissions, the decision was made to use the 89.9 kg/year figure but assign it a low degree of evidence quality.

Because no emissions data were reported for Hammerfest's WWTP (or for any other Arctic Norwegian WWTPs of similar size), the decision was made to use data for Kvalvikodden WWTP in Bodø, also a primary treatment plant discharging to marine receiving waters. Kvalvikodden reports copper emissions for 2021-2025. 2025's data were discarded as apparently incomplete at the time of reporting, and a mean (80.15 kg) calculated for 2021-2024. This mean was then adjusted for the population difference (10,488 (Hammerfest) divided by 49,780 (Bodø)), giving an average emission from WWTP of 16.89 kg/year [@statisticsnorway13144WastewaterPipelines2026]. Given the geography of the area and primary treatment, it seems likely that much of the copper deposited in Hammerfest municipality quickly reaches marine receiving waters, but without more specific assessment, this predicted WWTP emission provides a first-order, spatially non-specific estimate.

Reported emissions from the PRTR were averaged over the reported periods and grouped together as *Industrial emissions*. Although the methodology behind emission calculations is unclear and most relevant sites (13 of 18 in the municipality) do not report emissions, this KES was rated as moderately evidenced because the data were spatially relevant.

Sediment concentrations are well-described by existing data and predominantly below adverse effect thresholds; water concentration data are sparse but also largely below thresholds (of 13 data points, a single point falls within the Good-Moderate effect class). Tissue copper concentrations are available for *G. morhua* livers (largely below PROREF), *M. edulis* soft tissues (distributed around the PROREF boundary, but with some exceedances), and a handful of macroalgae (shoot tip) samples. Full node-level evidence and WoE scores underlying [@fig-hammerfest-aep] are available in the SI (@tbl-nodes-a001).

![Hammerfest Coastal System Aggregate Exposure Pathway (AEP). This AEP represents emissions from a variety of copper sources (orange Key Exposure States (KES)) to receiving marine water and sediment (blue KES), and eventually to Target Site Exposure (TSE) KES (pink), linked by Key Transitional Relationships (black and grey lines). Each KES reports a mean concentration emission (if available), sample size, number of references, date range, and a Weight of Evidence (WoE) assessment. WoE includes the Essentiality, Plausibility, Evidence, and Quantification of a given KES or KTR, scored 1-3 and colour-coded (adapted from [@pengAggregateExposurePathways2022]). Pin/globe icon in KES top-right corner indicates that a node is based on local (i.e. Hammerfest) or whole-Arctic data. Values rounded to 3 s.f.](figures/fig08-aep1-hammerfest.png){#fig-hammerfest-aep}

## AEP 2: Repparfjord System

Exposure data were likewise filtered to the Repparfjord study area. 8 groups of samples were returned, reflecting both national monitoring and two studies specifically scoped to the Repparfjord (see [@tbl-groups-a002], SI for more information). Although sediment contamination of the Repparfjord was well-covered in available data, data on concentrations in water in the fjord were unavailable, and a mean value for fjord water in the Norwegian Arctic was used in place. Available data for freshwater sediment (n = 1, 1600 mg/kg dry weight, sampled 2022 from a stream in historic mining area) were unusually high, and no data were available for the Repparfjord river. Consequently, Arctic-wide river water and sediment data were also used here, under the assumption that it was more relevant to represent Repparfjord river as a typical Norwegian Arctic river, rather than individual streams which may have highly localised patterns of contamination.

Spatial patterns ([@fig-aep2-conc]) of copper concentrations in the Repparfjord represent an extremely localised distribution of highly contaminated (Poor or Very Poor EQS) sediment samples to the inner fjord. Sediment samples in the mid and outer fjord are entirely classified as Background/Good, while none of the samples of species with PROREF values (which are extremely few) show exceedance of these reference values.

![Measured copper concentrations in specific compartments/organisms/tissue (with group numbers) in the Repparfjord system (AEP 2). Points shaped by sample group and coloured by worst measured concentration relative to (M-608) EQS or PROREF as appropriate. Red rectangle: AEP bounding box, Black square: Ulveryggen processing plant.](figures/fig07-aep2-concentrations.png){#fig-aep2-conc}

[@fig-a002-timeseries] shows insufficient ongoing monitoring of key sample groups to determine trends (although note that @sternalImpactSubmarineCopper2017 extracted sediment cores that give a historical overview of concentrations). Most sediment sampling captured occurred between 2010 and 2016, with only a single data point (recording an extremely high sediment concentration), while *G. morhua* and *M. edulis* tissue concentrations were only recorded in 2016.

![Measured copper concentrations over time in the Repparfjord system (AEP 2). Points coloured by EQS class/PROREF exceedance as appropriate. Dashed horizontal lines mark EQS/PROREF thresholds.  dw: dry weight, ww: wet weight.](figures/fig11-aep2-timeseries.png){#fig-a002-timeseries}

The Repparfjord AEP ([@fig-repparfjord-aep]) includes a small number of source KES, most notably the presence of almost 900 tonnes of copper in mine tailings at the floor of the inner fjord. Natural run-off to both the Repparfjord river (SE corner of the AEP) and the fjord itself is likely an important source of copper, but could not be quantified from available data. Anthropogenic run-off was included as an unquantified source. Although the area is sparsely populated, both sides of the fjord are bracketed by roads and the E6, Norway's main north-south highway, runs across the Repparfjord river plain, which means that brake wear may still be a relevant source of copper. Data for the part of Norway above the Arctic Circle were used to provide a rough estimate of likely copper concentrations in river water, river sediment, and fjord water. Measured copper levels in fjord sediment are, on average, much higher (74 ± 86.6 mg/kg (dry)) than those from Hammerfest (27.5 ± 59.9 mg/kg (dry)), driven by extremely high concentrations measured in the inner fjord. 

A larger number of biota tissue concentrations are available for this system, sourced from @kogelUsingAtlanticHaddock2026, although they represent sampling across a narrow time period. Fish liver concentrations of copper were on average higher (8.28 ± 6.94 mg/kg (wet)) than those measured in Hammerfest (6.22 ± 3.25 mg/kg (wet)), although the Repparfjord KES represents a wide range of species, none of which exceed the (*G. morhua*-specific) PROREF. Mussel data for Repparfjord are extremely sparse (n = 6) but give no indication that tailings disposal has affected tissue copper concentrations, which are lower (mean 1.04 ± 0.283 mg/kg (wet)) than those seen at Hammerfest (3.85 ± 8.92 mg/kg (wet)), albeit with the latter's mean driven by a pattern of occasional extremely high outliers. Crab muscle and hepatopancreas copper concentrations are consistently higher than mean tissue concentrations seen anywhere in Repparfjord or Hammerfest.

![Repparfjord system Aggregate Exposure Pathway (AEP). This AEP represents emissions from a variety of copper sources (orange Key Exposure States (KES)) to receiving marine water and sediment (blue KES), and eventually to Target Site Exposure (TSE) KES (pink), linked by Key Transitional Relationships (black and grey lines). Each KES reports a mean concentration emission (if available), sample size, number of references, date range, and a Weight of Evidence (WoE) assessment. WoE includes the Essentiality, Plausibility, Evidence, and Quantification of a given KES or KTR, scored 1-3 and colour-coded. Pin/globe icon in KES top-right corner indicates that a node is based on local (i.e. Hammerfest) or whole-Arctic data. Displayed quantities rounded to 3 s.f.](figures/fig10-aep2-repparfjord.png){#fig-repparfjord-aep}
